# Becker et al., early-2025 AI and experienced open-source developer productivity

**Source:** Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes and David Rein, "Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity". METR, arXiv:2507.09089v2, 25 Jul 2025. Licence CC BY 4.0 (per the arXiv abstract page). Scope: open.
**Structure:** A 51-page randomized controlled trial report. Introduction and background; methodology (developers and repositories, design, estimation, supplementary data); results (forecasts, activity labels, a 21-factor analysis); discussion and key caveats; appendices on misreadings and prior studies, each factor in detail, the empirical strategy, other analyses, primers on open-source development and AI tooling, and recruitment, instructions, surveys and labelling.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The authors randomize 246 real tasks from 16 experienced open-source developers, working in mature repositories they have contributed to for years, to allow or disallow AI tools at the February–June 2025 frontier, mostly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet (Abstract, p. 1). Developers forecast a 24% reduction in completion time and afterwards estimate a 20% reduction; with AI allowed, completion time actually rises by 19% (Abstract, p. 1). Economics and machine-learning experts predicted 39% and 38% reductions (Abstract, p. 1). Of 21 candidate factors, they find evidence that 5 contribute, mixed, unclear or no evidence for 10, and evidence against 6; experimental artifacts cannot be entirely ruled out, but the effect's robustness across analyses suggests it is unlikely to be mainly a product of the design (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2).

They bound the claim: the results do not imply that current AI is not useful in many realistic settings, that future models will not speed up developers here, or that better prompting, scaffolding or finetuning could not (§1, p. 3). What the results do show, they say, is a large disconnect between perceived and actual AI impact, with experts and developers drastically overestimating AI's usefulness even after many hours with the tools (§1, p. 3; §4, p. 10).

## Why This Study and How It Was Run

Lab experiments on synthetic tasks trade realism for scale and efficiency, and earlier field studies use outcomes such as lines of code, commits or pull requests that AI can move without productivity rising (§1, p. 1; §1.1, p. 3). Earlier studies report speedups of 21–65% on synthetic tasks and 14–51% on output measures; the authors place their study as the one, among those they compare, that combines AI at or above GPT-4, real tasks, experienced high-familiarity developers and a fixed outcome measure, with tasks defined before randomization (§1.1, pp. 3–4; App. B, pp. 17–18; §1, p. 2). Existing work finding that AI helps less experienced workers more motivates the focus on highly skilled developers (§1.1, p. 3).

Developers average 5 years and 1,500 commits on their repositories, which average 23,000 stars and 1,100,000 lines of code and broadly have very high quality bars; they are paid $150/hour (§2.1, p. 4). Each lists real issues, forecasts their time with and without AI, and has them randomized by simulated coin flip; with AI allowed they may use any tool or none, and with it disallowed no generative AI, including LLM autocomplete (§2.2, p. 5). They work in their own order, submit pull requests for normal review, and self-report time before and after review; they typically record their screens (§2.2, pp. 5–6; §2.2.2, p. 6). The estimate is the percentage change in completion time due to AI, from a log-linear regression controlling for the developer's pre-randomization forecast, with 95% intervals; the authors call positive values slowdown, which they flag as a mild abuse of language (§2.3, p. 6; App. D, pp. 28–31). Supplementary data include developer forecasts and post hoc estimates, incentivized expert forecasts, Cursor analytics, exit interviews and surveys, coded qualitative notes (which may carry bias from probing questions), and screen recordings labelled at about 10-second resolution, 74 of which (84 hours) are analysed after filtering (§2.4, pp. 7–8).

## Results

Developers complete 136 AI-allowed and 110 AI-disallowed issues, taking 19% longer with AI allowed, with nearly all quantiles of time longer; the confidence interval, read approximately from Figure 1, runs from about +1% to about +39%, and the caption does not state its level (§3, p. 8; Figure 1, p. 2). The raw difference in averages is 34%, larger because AI-allowed issues ended up slightly harder by forecast, a difference that is not statistically significant (§3.1, p. 9, footnote 12). Developers' forecasts still correlate with actual time (0.64 and 0.59): they are broadly well calibrated on relative issue length but their expectations about AI's usefulness are reversed (§3.1, p. 9). 75% of developers are slowed down, and on issues where developers forecast at least 33% speedup they are not slowed down (App. E.2, p. 32). With AI allowed, developers spend a smaller share of their time actively coding and reading or searching, and instead spend time reviewing AI output, prompting and waiting; they also spend a somewhat higher share idle (§3.2, pp. 9–10).

## Factors Behind the Slowdown

The authors sort 21 factors into direct productivity loss, experimental artifact, factors raising developer performance and factors limiting AI performance, and caution against over-indexing on any single piece of evidence, since subset analyses are not powered for multiple comparisons; the analysis is speculative and suggestive (§3.3, p. 10).

Five factors likely contribute (App. C.1, pp. 18–20). Over-optimism may lead developers to overuse AI despite its cost. High familiarity with the repositories matters: developers are slowed more on issues where they have high prior exposure and need few external resources (moderate evidence), and they say AI helps more on unfamiliar work. Large, complex repositories (about 10 years old, over 1,100,000 lines) limit AI, as developers report unwanted edits elsewhere in the code and edit failures one developer tied to file size. Reliability is low: developers accept under 44% of Cursor generations (3 developers on their own subscriptions excluded), 75% read every line of AI code, 56% often make major changes, and about 9% of AI-allowed time goes on reviewing and cleaning output. Developers say AI lacks the implicit, undocumented knowledge of the codebase they rely on.

Ten factors have unclear effect (App. C.2, pp. 20–25): overuse prompted by the experiment; a task sample tilted to smaller, possibly better-scoped issues; scope creep (developers reporting it are slowed less); completion order; recruitment bias against heavy AI users; trading speed for ease (69% keep using Cursor after the study); lower-quality initial pull requests (post-review time differs insignificantly, 15 against 9 minutes); below-average AI use (the authors see no meaningful difference by prior experience, excluding early AI-allowed issues changes little, and up to 50 hours of Cursor use more experience does not broadly reduce slowdown; one developer past 50 hours shows speedup, a later correction would move that bucket to roughly 0%, and the authors say more research is needed); generation latency (about 4% of time); and limited elicitation (normal use does not typically sample more than a few thousand tokens; alternative strategies untested).

Six factors are unlikely to contribute (App. C.3, pp. 25–28): an unfamiliar IDE (comparable-IDE subset still 24% slower); cheating or under-use (no AI in 16.4% of AI-allowed recordings, cheating in 3 of 54 disallowed); issue dropout (subsets 42%, 21%, 21%); the outcome measure (extreme imputation 14% and 23%, recording time 25% against 24%); the estimator (alternatives similar); and non-frontier models (mostly Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet, with most issues done in February and March 2025).

## Caveats and Misreadings

The authors caution against overgeneralizing: repository familiarity, size and maturity drive part of the slowdown and do not hold in many settings, and the results are consistent with small greenfield projects or unfamiliar codebases seeing substantial speedup (§4.1, p. 12). More reliable, faster or better-elicited AI could speed up developers in this setting, and preliminary evidence suggests autonomous agents can often implement the core functionality of issues in several study repositories while failing to satisfy all requirements, which they call immense progress over 1–2 years (§4.1, p. 12). They read the slowdown as some evidence that in-the-wild capability may be lower than benchmarks suggest, and the overestimates as a reason for field experiments over expert forecasts or developer surveys alone (§4, pp. 10–12). Table 2 lists what the study does not show: that AI fails to speed up many or most developers, people outside software, future models in this setting, better-used current tools, much more experienced AI users, or these developers on every task (App. B, p. 17).

## Procedures and Instruments

Forecasted difficulty is balanced across conditions, and assignment (55.3% against 44.7%) does not differ significantly from 50/50; 25 early block-randomized issues do not change the result (App. E.1, E.3, pp. 31–33). Recruitment drew on networks, Reddit and GitHub, filtered to active contributors to repositories with over 500 stars; three developers were later excluded (App. G, G.6, pp. 37, 45). Hourly pay was chosen over per-issue bonuses that could bias behaviour (App. G.1, p. 37). The appendices reproduce the developer instructions (eligibility, issue fields including Prior Task Exposure and External Resource Needs, time tracking, perceived effort), onboarding and check-ins, the exit interview outline and survey, the labelling instructions, and the brief given to expert forecasters, written mid-study (App. G.2–G.9, pp. 37–51).

## Key Statistics

- 16 developers; 246 tasks (136 AI-allowed, 110 AI-disallowed); 2.0 hours average (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2; §3, p. 8).
- Completion time with AI allowed: +19%; Figure 1 interval about +1% to +39% (approximate, read from the figure; level not stated) (§3, p. 8; Figure 1, p. 2).
- Forecasts: developers −24% before, −20% after; economics experts −39% (n = 34), machine-learning experts −38% (n = 54) (§3.1, pp. 8–9).
- Raw ratio 34%; forecast–actual correlations 0.64 and 0.59; 75% of developers slowed (§3.1, p. 9; App. E.2, p. 32).
- Cursor generations accepted: under 44% (excluding 3 developers on their own subscriptions); time reviewing and cleaning AI output about 9%, waiting about 4% (App. C.1.4, p. 20; App. C.2.9, p. 25).
- Prior experience: 93% with LLMs, 44% with Cursor; 69% keep using Cursor after the study (§2.2.1, p. 6; App. C.2.6, p. 23).
- Factors: 21 examined; 5 contribute, 10 unclear, 6 not (§3.3, p. 10).

## Key Connections

- Peng et al., Paradis et al., Weber et al.: speedups on synthetic tasks; Peng et al.'s task called unrepresentative of most software development work and likely similar to a large amount of LLM training data, which may unfairly advantage AI (§1.1, p. 3).
- Gambacorta et al., Yeverechyahu et al., Cui et al.: output gains on measures not fixed in advance (§1.1, p. 3; App. B, p. 18).
- Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb on AI as cheaper prediction; Brynjolfsson et al., Noy and Zhang, Choi and Schwarcz on AI helping less experienced workers more (§1.1, p. 3).
- Benchmark literature and critiques of lab tasks; environment-complexity literature (§1, p. 1; App. C.1.3, p. 19).
- Kwa et al. on the pace of AI progress (§1, p. 3).
- DellaVigna et al. on forecasting experiments; Gneiting and Raftery on scoring rules; Abadie et al. and cluster-robust inference papers (§2.4, p. 7; App. D.2, p. 28).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Lab experiments on synthetic tasks sacrifice realism and make it difficult to infer real-world impact (§1, p. 1).
2. Outcome measures not fixed in advance, such as lines of code, commits or pull requests, can rise without productivity rising (§1.1, p. 3).
3. Relying solely on expert forecasts or developer surveys, rather than field experiments with robust outcome measures (§4, p. 12).
4. Benchmarks fail to measure how much models speed up engineers in their real workflow (App. G.2.1, pp. 38–39).
5. This study's result should not be over-generalized (App. B, p. 17; §4.1, p. 12).
